claims.text: As-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high-entropy-alloy thin films can be produced under identical sputtering conditions.
The magnetocaloric response and hysteresis of these films during low-field cycling are governed by substrate-mediated heat-removal efficiency.
Films on high-thermal-conductivity substrates will have a sharper magnetocaloric transition than films on low-thermal-conductivity substrates.
Films on high-thermal-conductivity substrates will have less magnetic hysteresis than films on low-thermal-conductivity substrates.
RF or magnetron sputtering in an inert argon atmosphere is an applicable deposition route for the proposed HEA films.
Sapphire or diamond can serve as the high-thermal-conductivity substrates, while SiO2 can serve as the low-thermal-conductivity substrate.
Substrate thermal properties govern local heat dissipation during magnetic-field cycling.
Substrate-dependent heat dissipation modulates the formation and relaxation of thermal gradients within the film.
High-thermal-conductivity substrates rapidly remove heat generated during magnetic-cooling cycles.
Rapid heat removal limits local temperature overshoots in the film.
Local temperature overshoots can cause spatially non-uniform magnetic-domain nucleation and growth.
Efficient heat extraction produces a more abrupt magnetocaloric transition.
Efficient heat extraction reduces hysteresis associated with magnetic-domain-wall dynamics.
Low-thermal-conductivity substrates produce slower heat removal and more persistent thermal gradients.
Persistent thermal gradients broaden the transition and increase hysteresis.
Standard FeMnNiGeSi-film substrates are typically low in thermal conductivity, with SiO2 given as an example.
The proposed effect applies to films tens to a few hundred nanometers thick under low magnetic fields near the phase-transition temperature.
Within the proposed operating range, substrate heat conduction can alter local temperature gradients without extraneous interfacial effects dominating.
The substrate effect may be subtle and must be separated from interfacial and processing artifacts.
